title: Investigate an Unexpected Oscillation in a Controlled Experiment
problem: A precision sensor began oscillating after its control software changed. Is this a physical signal, an instrument or software artifact, or coincidence? The raw observations, calibration records, environmental logs, and software history are missing; identifying what evidence is needed is part of the investigation. Form competing hypotheses spanning genuine physical effects, instrument artifacts, environmental coupling, aliasing, software defects, and statistical coincidence. Design a preregisterable, blinded where feasible investigation: identify indispensable measurements and metadata, controls, sample-size and power assumptions, quantitative analyses, falsification tests, replication criteria, and how to handle multiple comparisons. Explicitly distinguish simulated or proposed observations from actual evidence. Do not claim that a novel physical effect exists without data. Deliver a ranked experimental plan, predicted signatures of each hypothesis, decision rules, and unresolved uncertainties.

strategies.title: Turn the question into a test
strategies.approach: Name the proposed cause, measurable outcome, comparison condition, and one plausible confounder. Write a prediction that could fail, then sketch the smallest ethical observation or experiment that would distinguish it from a competing explanation.
strategies.summary: Turn the question into a test

strategies.title: Audit evidence before concluding
strategies.approach: For one available claim, trace the measurement to its source, check whether the comparison supports causation, and list a result that would weaken the claim. Keep observation, interpretation, and established conclusion in separate notes.
